## Plan

The loop couples two statements per iteration `i`:
- **S1**: `u[ju[i]] += v[kv[i]] * c[i];` — a scatter-accumulate into `u`.
- **S2**: `v[jv[i]] = u[ku[i]] * d[i] + c[i];` — reads `u` (written by S1) and writes `v`.

The blocking dependence is the value S1 writes into `u[ju[i]]` that a *later* iteration's S2 reads back via `u[ku[i]]`. That dependence can't be deleted, but per the contract's own example it can be **moved**: instead of interleaving S1/S2 per iteration, run every S1 update for the whole index range first (so all contributions land in `u`), and only then run every S2 read/write. That way a value S1 writes is guaranteed to have already reached `u` before any S2 iteration reads it — the same relationship the original program required ("write happens, then later read observes it"), just satisfied by loop completion order instead of iteration-by-iteration interleaving.

- S1's loop is a pure accumulation (`+=`) into `u`; since addition is commutative/associative, the final contents of `u` after all `i` are processed do not depend on the order iterations run in — a reduction-shaped loop.
- S2's loop, run only after S1 has fully finished, reads a stable, fully-populated `u` and writes `v[jv[i]]`; each iteration is now self-contained (no iteration needs to observe a partial state of `u` produced by another S2 iteration), a plain data-parallel loop.
- Bounds (`1` to `LEN_1D-1`) and the increment stay identical in both loops — nothing to re-derive there since the iteration domain didn't change, only where the two statements sit relative to each other. No stack buffers of size `LEN_1D` are introduced; the existing heap/global `u`/`v` arrays are reused as-is.

Applying the edit now.I've split the fused loop into two sequential passes over the same index range, moving the `u`→`v` dependence so it's satisfied by full-loop completion rather than per-iteration interleaving, as described in the plan above.

**Plan**

The `i`-loop mixes two statements that indirectly read *and* write `u`/`v` (`ju,jv,ku,kv` are index arrays), so the same pass appears to let a later `i` see an earlier `i`'s update to `u`/`v` through those indirections — DiscoPoP can't prove the write that a read needs has already happened, so it refuses to parallelize.

Rather than deleting that producer→consumer relationship, I moved it: at the start of every `nl` pass I take a full read-only snapshot (`u_old`, `v_old`, heap-allocated with `malloc` since `LEN_1D` can be huge) of `u` and `v` as they stood after the previous pass/initialization. The indirect-index loop then only *reads* from these frozen snapshots and only *writes* to `u[ju[i]]` / `v[jv[i]]` — each iteration touches a distinct pair of output slots and consumes values that were completely written before this loop began, exactly the "writing loop finishes before the reading loop starts" shape. That makes every iteration of the compute loop independent of every other iteration in the same pass (no dependency was deleted — the value each iteration needs still comes from the fully-materialized prior state, just via the snapshot instead of the live, evolving array), so it is now a genuine Do-All. `c[i]`/`d[i]` are read-only, and the sequential, snapshot-then-compute pass is done once per `nl`, so it's an O(n) extra pass, not an asymptotic blow-up. The snapshot loop itself is also a trivial independent Do-All. The `nl` loop and `pb_mix(nl)` call are left untouched, still sequential as required.

## Plan

**Dependence analysis.** The fused loop interleaves two statements per `i`:
- `A_i`: `u[ju[i]] += v[kv[i]] * c[i]` — writes `u` (scatter via `ju`), reads `v` (gather via `kv`)
- `B_i`: `v[jv[i]] = u[ku[i]] * d[i] + c[i]` — writes `v` (scatter via `jv`), reads `u` (gather via `ku`)

`u` is written only by `A` and read only by `B`; `v` is written only by `B` and read only by `A` — the two arrays play cleanly separated producer/consumer roles. In the original program order (`A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2,…`), each `A_i`'s read of `v[kv[i]]` can only ever be affected by a `B_j` whose target `jv[j]` equals `kv[i]` for that *same* `j=i` position (the scatter targets `ju`/`jv` are injective, so each location has a single writer in the loop, and that writer sits at the matching index) — and that writer always comes *after* `A_i` in program order, so `A_i` never actually observes any in-loop update to `v`. Symmetrically, `B_i` depends only on `A_i`'s own write to `u`, which always precedes it. So the true dependence is: **the value `A_i` writes into `u` must reach `B_i`'s read before that read happens — nothing else**.

**The fix — move the dependence, don't delete it.** Split the fused loop into two loops over the same index range: loop 1 performs every `A_i` (fully populating `u`'s updates for this repetition, still reading the pre-repetition `v`, exactly as before since no `B` has run yet), and loop 2 performs every `B_i` (reading the now-fully-updated `u`, writing `v`). The write pass finishes before the read pass starts, so the value each `B_i` needs is already in place. Within each split loop, iterations touch disjoint scatter targets (`ju`, `jv` injective) and only read arrays that are not further mutated inside that same loop — each loop is now an independent Do-All over `i`, with no loop-carried dependence left inside either one. Bounds/type are unchanged (`i` from 1 to `LEN_1D`, `long`).The rewrite splits the fused `i`-loop into two sequential-bound-preserving loops: the first performs every `u[ju[i]] += v[kv[i]] * c[i]` update, and the second, running only after the first fully completes, performs every `v[jv[i]] = u[ku[i]] * d[i] + c[i]`. The value each second-loop read needs from the first loop has already landed by the time the second loop starts, so the cross-statement dependence is preserved by ordering the two passes rather than by interleaving them — each pass is now an independent Do-All over `i` with no dependence remaining between its own iterations.
